report.answer: The three least-adaptation transfers are: (1) Nextflow-style hash-keyed resume with completed-state and output validation; (2) Slurm-style indexed fan-out, receipt-state dependency predicates and a separate accounting ledger; and (3) LOOT-style hard/soft constraint graphs with cycle rejection and deterministic topological ordering. Ghidra headless phases and OpenCue frame control transfer with more rewriting. Ghidra BSim is the negative control and is not transferable because its decompiler-derived feature/confidence core would have to be replaced.

claims.statement: All six scanned mechanisms are first-class capabilities in canonical community tool documentation or source; this supports tool-standard practice but does not measure community-wide adoption prevalence.
Nextflow implements hash-keyed resume with completed-state and cached-output checks; adapting it requires three named component rewrites and is the lowest-cost transfer in this scan.
Slurm's indexed arrays, afterok/aftercorr predicates and accounting surface transfer after four named component rewrites and rank second by the declared rubric.
LOOT's hard/soft constraint graph, cycle control and deterministic topological ordering transfer after five named component rewrites and rank third by the declared rubric.
Ghidra Headless Analyzer's ordered pre/main/post lifecycle and explicit continuation control are transferable, but six named component rewrites make it a moderate-cost fourth-place candidate.
OpenCue's job/layer/frame dependencies and granular retry state are transferable, but seven named component rewrites make it a moderate-cost fifth-place candidate.
Ghidra BSim is the negative-control mechanism: its decompiler-derived feature and confidence model requires eight core rewrites, so it is not transferable rather than merely expensive.
Applying the declared rewrite-count rubric yields Nextflow content cache, Slurm array/dependency/accounting and LOOT constraint graph as the three least-adaptation transfers, in that order.
